sections.overview: Cassida rubiginosa is a tortoise beetle in the leaf-beetle family Chrysomelidae, native across much of the Palearctic and introduced in parts of North America.
sections.identification: The adults are flattened and shield-like, with expanded margins of the pronotum and wing covers; larvae carry a shield made from shed skins and feces.
sections.habitat: It is associated with thistles and other Asteraceae in open habitats, including field edges and disturbed ground.
sections.diet: Adults and larvae feed on foliage, especially Canada thistle Cirsium arvense, and several other thistle relatives.
sections.behavior: Adults overwinter in litter, emerge in spring, feed and mate; the species normally has one generation per year.
sections.reproduction: Eggs are laid on leaves and larvae pass through five instars before pupating on the host plant.
sections.ecology: It is closely related to other Cassida tortoise beetles, including C. stigmatica; host-plant breadth and larval shield traits help distinguish these congeners.
sections.conservation: It has been studied as a biological-control agent against invasive Canada thistle, but field effects can be modest and depend on other herbivores and site conditions.
